svg.aria-label: Diagram: passwordless authentication on Microsoft Entra, comparing device-bound and synced passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and Microsoft Authenticator, showing what each credential binds to, why origin binding is what defeats phishing, the attestation trade that excludes synced passkeys, and the Temporary Access Pass bootstrap problem of registering a passwordless credential when the user has none
svg.title: Every passwordless method is the same idea: a private key that cannot leave, bound to one origin
svg.text: One idea, four packages: a private key that cannot leave, bound to one origin.
The differences are where the key lives and who vouches for it — which is also the whole of the attestation argument.
What each credential actually binds to
METHOD
WHERE THE PRIVATE KEY LIVES
MOVES BETWEEN DEVICES?
FIDO2 security key
the key itself, never leaves it
no — you carry the hardware
Passkey in Microsoft Authenticator
iOS Secure Enclave; Android Secure
Element, or the TEE as fallback
no — device-bound by design
Windows Hello for Business
the device TPM, unlocked by a gesture
no — one credential per device
Synced passkey (iCloud, Google)
created in an HSM, encrypted, then
stored with the cloud passkey provider
yes — that is the point, and
the reason attestation excludes it
Why it cannot be phished, in one sentence
“A private key is stored on your device and public key is stored with the app or the website that you sign into … This key pair
combination is unique, so your passkey only works on the website or the app you created it for.”
A relay site is a different origin, so the key simply does not answer it. And “every sign-in attempt requires that you’re present to
unlock the passkey on the device that you use for sign in” — there is no code to read out to anybody.
The attestation trade
Attestation proves which authenticator model created
the key, through the FIDO Metadata Service.
“If attestation is enabled, only device-bound passkeys
are allowed; synced passkeys are excluded.”
So it is not a security dial you simply turn up. It is a
choice between knowing the device and letting the
credential follow the user.
What Microsoft measured on synced passkeys
99% of users successfully register them
14x faster than password plus traditional MFA —
3 seconds instead of 69 seconds
3x more successful at signing in than legacy
methods — 95% against 30%
From consumer Microsoft accounts, not enterprise.
The bootstrap problem: registering a passwordless credential needs a credential
Temporary Access Pass
a time-limited passcode. Default 1 hour, 8 characters; 10 minutes
to 30 days allowed, length 8–48
The ten-minute rule
with a one-time TAP, registration “must be completed within 10
minutes of sign-in” — device enrolment alone can outrun that
One per user
“Each user can only have one TAP”; a new one overrides the old
It does not replace the password
“Users can also continue to sign in by using their password”
And the token lifetime carries over: tokens issued during a TAP sign-in “have their maximum lifetime capped at the TAP expiration
time” — but “TAP expiration doesn’t retroactively invalidate sessions that are already established”, so a session can outlive the pass.
Sources: Passkeys (FIDO2) in Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Authenticator authentication method, Windows Hello for Business overview, and Temporary Access Pass, on Microsoft Learn.
